doc.title: Dave Liebman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: How the music was built: bass lines, Michael Henderson and Pete Cosey
summary: Miles's pieces began from bass lines and short melodies; they discuss Michael Henderson, Reggie Lucas and Pete Cosey's blues and AACM background.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: Let’s break here. He’s running on the end. He needs to switch. Whatever “tunes” there were, or material, or whatever, Miles brought in, and Miles conducted.

Yes. It started with a bass line, and the drums would start. He’d just play a little melody. The melody, there was nothing more than two bars. Maybe there was a four-bar melody. There was one melody – one longer melody.
Even that music going back to Bitches Brew, most of it is based on bass things, like Bitches Brew or Miles Runs the Voodoo Down, or whatever.

Exactly. That’s the point. That’s what he was pursuing. It came from the bass, in the end. And Sly – that’s why this line from Sly was great. It was very slippery, a slippery bass line, no real 1. Although Michael Henderson was much more rudimentary than that. The thing that made Michael Henderson great, I thought, was that he was very simple and he laid it right down. He did not play that fast stuff. He was not – Jaco was not a thing yet, but he was not coming out of any of that stuff. He didn’t even play like Chuck Rainey. He played much simpler than anybody, Michael.

He was a Motown prodigy, of Jamerson. He was Jamerson’s protégé, Jamie Jamerson, who was the main guy. Very simple and very solid and very literal. I think that – Miles would just work off of the sound of the guitar. Reggie just played any kind of comp. The main soloists were me and Pete Cosey, besides Miles.
Cosey’s from Chicago. Played with Gene Ammons before he was with Miles.
I always think of him as a really out player.
